## Dataset: Grassland restoration: insects and insect traits

This dataset contains all data, on which the following publication below is based.<br>&#42;&#42;Paper Citation&#42;&#42;:<br>Neff, F., Resch, M. C., Marty, A., Rolley, J. D., Schütz, M., Risch, A. C, Gossner, M. M. 2020. Long-term restoration success of insect herbivore communities in semi-natural grasslands: a functional approach. Ecological Applications, 30, e02133. &#91;10.1002/eap.2133&#93;&#40;https://doi.org/10.1002/eap.2133&#41;<br>Please cite this paper together with the citation for the datafile.<br> Methods<br> Study site<br>The study area is situated within and nearby to Eigental nature reserve &#40;47°27’36” to 47°29’06” N, 8°37’12” to 8°37’44” E, 461 to 507 m a.s.l.&#41; in the vicinity of Zurich airport &#40;Canton Zurich, Switzerland&#41;. Mean annual precipitation and temperature is 903 ± 136 mm and 9.14°C ± 0.50°C &#40;mean ± SD for 2007-2017 &#40;&#42;MeteoSchweiz 2018&#42;&#41;&#41;. In 1967, the Eigental nature reserve was established to protect small and isolated remnants of species-rich, semi-natural grasslands &#40;roughly 12 ha&#41;, which were embedded in an otherwise intensively managed landscape. It is characterized by oligo- to mesotrophic Molinion &#40;semi-wet, matrix species &#42;Molinia caerulea&#42;&#41; and Mesobromion &#40;semi-dry, matrix species &#42;Bromus erectus&#42;&#41; meadows &#40;&#42;Delarze et al. 2015&#42;&#41;, reflecting small-scale habitat heterogeneity, mainly due to site-specific groundwater levels and slope inclination. As in most Central European grasslands, management is necessary to prevent shrub and tree invasions as well as to secure low levels of available soil nutrients and thus to maintain these species-rich habitats &#40;&#91;&#42;Poschlod and WallisDeVries 2002&#42;&#93;&#40;https://doi.org/10.1016/S0006-3207&#40;01&#41;00201-4&#41;&#41;.<br>In 1990, the government of the Canton Zurich decided to enlarge the Eigental nature reserve as a counter measure against degradation and biodiversity loss in semi-natural grasslands due to overutilization and the excessive input of nutrients &#40;mostly nitrogen&#41;. Eleven patches of adjacent intensively managed grassland &#40;in total roughly 20 ha&#41; were targeted to be transformed into semi-natural grasslands. As a first restoration measure, fertilization was ceased, and biomass harvested three times to remove excessive soil nutrients from the original system and thus benefit plant species with low competitive ability on the long run. In 1995, the restoration efforts were increased and a large-scale experiment comprising three restoration measures with increasing intervention intensities was implemented:<br>- &#42;&#42;Harvest only&#42;&#42;: Initial restoration measures were continued with mowing and removing of the aboveground biomass two times a year &#40;early summer and autumn&#41;.<br>- &#42;&#42;Topsoil&#42;&#42;: Removal of topsoil, depending on the thickness of the A horizon the upper 10 to 20 cm, in four randomly selected areas within the eleven patches in late autumn 1995. The size of the restoration area depended on individual patch size &#40;2700 to 7000 m2&#41;.<br>- &#42;&#42;Topsoil + Propagules&#42;&#42;: Plant propagules were added on half of the area where topsoil was removed via application of fresh, seed-containing hay and hand-collected propagules of target species originating from semi-dry and semi-wet species-rich grasslands with local and regional provenance &#40;within radius of 7 to 30 km&#41; &#40;1995, 1996, 1997&#41;.<br>Management of &#42;Topsoil&#42; and &#42;Topsoil + Propagules&#42; started five years after treatment implementation and included yearly mowing and removing of aboveground biomass &#40;late summer or early autumn&#41;. The experiment was complemented with intensively managed grassland sites that share the same agricultural history as the restored sites &#40;&#42;&#42;Initial&#42;&#42;; swards dominated by &#42;Lolium perenne&#42;, &#42;L. multiflorum&#42; and &#42;Trifolium repens&#42;&#41;: mowing and subsequent fertilizing &#40;manure&#41; up to five times a year, as well as different tillage regimes. Finally, sites were selected in target semi-dry and semi-wet grasslands &#40;&#42;&#42;Target&#42;&#42;&#41; located within the Eigental nature reserve and another nature reserve nearby &#40;Altläufe der Glatt; 47°28’29” to 47°27’41” N, 8°31’56” to 8°32’26” E, 418 to 420 m a.s.l.&#41;. The selected target sites are mown and aboveground biomass removed once a year in late summer or early autumn. For each of the five treatments, we selected eleven plots &#40;5 m × 5 m&#41; spread across the sites. Altogether, the experiment included 55 plots.<br> Arthropod sampling<br>Aboveground arthropods were sampled using suction sampling on four consecutive days in early July 2017 before the grasslands were mown. Arthropods were sampled in two locations on each 5 m × 5 m plot, once in the south-western and once in the north-eastern corner to account for possible spatial heterogeneity within the plots. Arthropods were sorted to order or lower taxonomic levels and individuals were identified to species level. We focused on three groups &#40;Hemiptera: Auchenorrhyncha, Hemiptera: Heteroptera, Orthoptera&#41;,<br> Functional traits<br>We used two sets of functional traits in this study.  <br>&#42;&#42;Morphometric traits&#42;&#42;:  <br>Body volume, body shape, hind femur shape, hind/front leg ratio, wing length, leg length, antenna length and eye width. We used trait measurements from &#91;&#42;Simons et al. &#40;2016&#41;&#42;&#93;&#40;http://dx.doi.org/10.1890/15-0616.1&#41; and &#91;&#42;Neff et al. &#40;2019&#41;&#42;&#93;&#40;https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-019-00872-1&#41; and complemented them with measurements on study specimens. These measurements were conducted using a high-resolution measuring stereo microscope &#40;Leica DVM6, Leica Microsystems&#41; including automated high-resolution photo stacking with the software Leica Application Suite X &#40;LAS X, © 2018 Leica Microsystems CMS GmbH&#41; and Leica Map Premium &#40;Leica Microsystems, © 1996-2017 Digital Surf&#41; at WSL Birmensdorf. The eight morphometric traits were calculated from direct measurements of body parts on specimens of all sampled species. From each species, we measured at least one female and one male specimen. Additionally, for species that show wing dimorphism, we included the different wing morphs and weighted them by their prevalence reported in literature. For few species, of which not all wing morphs were available for measurements &#40;10 cases&#41;, we estimated relative wing length from congeneric species or from the literature.  <br>&#42;&#42;Life-history traits&#42;&#42;  <br>Based on an existing data set collected by &#91;&#42;Gossner et al. &#40;2015&#41;&#42;&#93;&#40;http://dx.doi.org/10.1890/14-2159.1&#41;. We included traits describing different life-history characteristics of herbivore insect species, namely: feeding specialization, feeding tissue, hibernation stage and number of generations per year, which are related to insect species’ vulnerability to changes in plant community composition, microhabitat use and disturbance tolerance. To represent potential changes in habitat moisture with abandonment of intensive land use &#40;e.g., change in ground-water level&#41;, we also included two traits related to preferred habitat moisture of the study species: moisture preference, describing species’ optimum habitat moisture, and moisture range, which describes the species’ range of preferable moisture conditions.  <br> References<br>Delarze, R., Y. Gonseth, S. Eggenberg, and M. Vust. 2015. Lebensräume der Schweiz: Ökologie - Gefährdung - Kennarten. 3rd ed. Ott, Bern.  <br>Gossner, M. M., N. K. Simons, R. Achtziger, T. Blick, W. H. O. Dorow, F. Dziock, F. Köhler, W. Rabitsch, and W. W. Weisser. 2015. A summary of eight traits of Coleoptera, Hemiptera, Orthoptera and Araneae, occurring in grasslands in Germany. Scientific Data 2:150013.  <br>MeteoSchweiz. 2018. Klimabulletin Jahr 2017. MeteoSchweiz, Zürich.  <br>Neff, F., N. Blüthgen, M. N. Chisté, N. K. Simons, J. Steckel, W. W. Weisser, C. Westphal, L. Pellissier, and M. M. Gossner. 2019. Cross-scale effects of land use on the functional composition of herbivorous insect communities. Landscape Ecology 34:2001–2015.  <br>Poschlod, P., and M. F. ## Load packages

This template targets tidyverse (2.x) and skimr (2.x) with R 4.1 or newer for the native `|>` pipe; package versions are not pinned. Install missing packages once with `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "skimr"))`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

USER_AGENT <- "OpendataSwiss-StarterCode-R/1.0"
HTTP_TIMEOUT <- 30

get_dataset <- function(url, delim = NULL, drop_empty_unnamed = TRUE, ...) {
  if (grepl("^https?://", url)) {
    local_file <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(local_file), add = TRUE)
    old_options <- options(timeout = HTTP_TIMEOUT)
    on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
    status <- download.file(url, local_file, method = "libcurl", mode = "wb",
                            quiet = TRUE, headers = c("User-Agent" = USER_AGENT))
    if (status != 0) stop("Resource download failed")
    url <- local_file
  }
  data <- read_delim(url, delim = delim, show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
  stop_for_problems(data)
  if (drop_empty_unnamed && nrow(data) > 0) {
    # Blank CSV headers (often from trailing separators) become "...n".
    unnamed <- grepl("^\\.\\.\\.[0-9]+$", names(data))
    empty_unnamed <- unnamed & map_lgl(data, ~ all(is.na(.x)))
    if (any(empty_unnamed)) {
      message("Removed empty unnamed columns: ", paste(names(data)[empty_unnamed], collapse = ", "))
      data <- data[, !empty_unnamed, drop = FALSE]
    }
  }
  data
}
```

For CSV, the delimiter and column types are guessed. Check the preview and metadata; set `delim`, `col_types`, `na`, or `locale` in `get_dataset(...)` when needed (for example, read identifiers with leading zeros as character columns). Parsing problems stop the import so they can be addressed.

## Missing values

```{r missing-values}
missing <- tibble(
  column = names(df),
  missing = map_int(df, ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
  missing_pct = map_dbl(df, ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_pct))
missing

# Show up to 20 columns with missing values; percentages use all rows.
missing_plot <- missing |> filter(missing > 0) |> slice_head(n = 20)
if (nrow(missing_plot) > 0) {
  ggplot(missing_plot, aes(x = missing_pct, y = reorder(column, missing_pct))) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = "Missing values (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missingness by column")
} else {
  message("No missing values to plot (or the dataset has no rows).")
}
```

## Summary and distributions

`skim()` reports completeness and type-specific summaries. Inspect units before interpreting numeric codes as measurements.

```{r summary}
if (nrow(df) > 0 && ncol(df) > 0) {
  skim(df)
} else {

```

```{r histograms}
# Plot up to four numeric columns, excluding non-finite values only from plots.
numeric_names <- names(select(df, where(is.numeric))) |> head(4)
for (column in numeric_names) {
  values <- df[[column]]
  values <- values[is.finite(values)]
  if (length(values) > 0) {
    plot <- ggplot(tibble(value = values), aes(x = value)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
      labs(title = column, x = column, y = "Count")
    print(plot)
  }
}
```

```{r category-counts}
# Top 10 values for up to three categorical columns, including missing values.
categorical_names <- df |>
  select(where(~ is.character(.x) || is.factor(.x) || is.logical(.x))) |>
  names() |>
  head(3)
for (column in categorical_names) {
  cat(column, "\n")
  df |> count(.data[[column]], sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> print()
}
```
